It won’t be a single crisp number (too many unknowns), but we can bound it with clean physics. --- Minimum Radiated Power estimate (GNSS L1/L2/L5 interference) Step 1: What the receiver needs to be overwhelmed GPS signals arrive at the aircraft antenna extremely weak (think “whisper from orbit”): roughly -130 dBm-ish at the receiver front end (order-of-magnitude). A jammer doesn’t need to “beat” GPS by a little, it needs to raise the noise floor enough that the receiver loses correlation and/or flags integrity. A useful forensic knob is required J/S (jam-to-signal ratio). For many civilian receivers, ~20–40 dB of advantage in-band is enough to cause loss of lock or severe degradation, depending on bandwidth, antenna, and receiver design. So a crude “receiver disruption power” target is: If GPS is ~-130 dBm, then: Jammer at receiver ~-110 dBm (20 dB J/S) → mild-to-serious degradation possible ~-90 dBm (40 dB J/S) → hard failure is plausible We’ll compute both. --- Step 2: Free-space path loss at 10 miles Assume the interfering emitter is roughly line-of-sight at 10 miles ≈ 16 km, frequency ~1.575 GHz (GPS L1). Free-space path loss: \text{FSPL(dB)} \approx 32.45 + 20\log_{10}(f_{\text{MHz}}) + 20\log_{10}(d_{\text{km}}) Plug in MHz, km: \text{FSPL} \approx 32.45 + 63.94 + 24.08 \approx 120.47 \text{ dB} Call it ~120.5 dB. --- Step 3: Convert “needed received power” to transmitter EIRP EIRP (effective isotropic radiated power) is: \text{EIRP(dBm)} \approx P_{\text{rx}}(\text{dBm}) + \text{FSPL(dB)} Case A: Receiver disruption at -110 dBm (moderate) \text{EIRP} \approx -110 + 120.5 = 10.5 \text{ dBm} Case B: Receiver disruption at -90 dBm (harder failure) \text{EIRP} \approx -90 + 120.5 = 30.5 \text{ dBm} Case C: Receiver disruption at -80 dBm (very strong) \text{EIRP} \approx -80 + 120.5 = 40.5 \text{ dBm} So the minimum EIRP to plausibly cause a rapid integrity collapse at 10 miles is often in the ballpark of: ~10 mW to ~10 W EIRP (broad-brush), depending on receiver robustness and jammer bandwidth. That sounds “too small,” but it’s because GPS is astonishingly weak at the receiver. --- The big gotcha: bandwidth (this can raise power needs by a lot) If the interference is wideband noise over, say, 10 MHz, you need more total power than if it’s a narrow spike or a structured spoofing waveform. Rule of thumb: Wideband barrage jamming generally costs more power. Spoofing can be effective at relatively low power if it’s coherent and well-timed. So those watt estimates are minimums for in-band effective power at the receiver, not guaranteed real-world totals. --- Why “NIC 8 → 0 in under 2 seconds” points to jamming/spoofing onset That rapid collapse is consistent with: sudden noise floor jump (jamming), sudden false correlation lock (spoofing), or sudden antenna/view obstruction. It’s not proof of EW by itself, but it is consistent with it. --- Practical Lane A next step (tightest version) If you want this to be more than a back-of-envelope: 1. Decide a working range: 5 mi, 10 mi, 20 mi 2. Decide interference type: narrowband, wideband, spoofing-like 3. Include antenna gains (aircraft GNSS antenna gain and emitter gain) 4. Add a margin: +10 to +20 dB (real-world losses, polarization mismatch, clutter) Then we output a power band like: “Minimum plausible EIRP” “Likely EIRP with real-world losses” “High-confidence EIRP if wideband” If you tell me just one assumption: narrowband vs wideband, I’ll give you the final bounded range with margins.
